thread.title: After the Bell: 488 Losers, from Amazon to Tesla - Barron's

author: Brett Arends
title: After the Bell: 488 Losers, from Amazon to Tesla - Barron's
text:
By Brett Arends April 6, 2018 6:18 p.m. ET Illustration: Getty Images Twelve.
That’s the total number of stocks in the Standard & Poor’s 500 index that rose today, as more talk of a trade war and mixed signals from the White House led to a rout in the markets.
Most of the winners weren't widely held.
As for the other 488, including all 30 components of the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the picture wasn't pretty. The Dow plunged 572 points to finish the session at 23,933, although it bounced off a session low of 23,738. The S&P closed down 58 at 2604, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.28% to 7,481. But the small-cap Russell 2000 shed only 0.49% to 1,576.
Among the biggest names, Apple ( AAPL ) fell $4.42 to $168.38, Tesla ( TSLA ) $6.42 to $29.30, Alphabet ( GOOGL ) $22.69 to $1009.95, Facebook ( FB ) $2.14 to $157.20, and Netflix ( NFLX ) $5.12 to $288.85.
Major energy companies suffered as trade-war fears knocked oil prices down 2.5% to $62 a barrel. Exxon Mobil ( XOM ) was down $1.15 to $74.87 and Chevron ( CVX ) was off $2.53 to $114.76. Amazon.com ( AMZN ) tumbled $46.52 to $1405.23 as Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin backed up the president’s political war on the company, whose CEO, Jeff Bezos, owns the Washington Post.
Companies considered economic bellwethers also fared poorly. Wal-Mart (WMT) fell $1.12 to $86.69, Bank of America ( BAC ) $0.69 to $29.63, and Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) $2.61 to $128.10. Gold, meanwhile, rose 0.6% to $1337 an ounce.
Treasury Secretary Mnuchin made a bad situation worse when he went on CNBC’s Power Lunch and said yes, “there is a potential of a trade war.” For good measure he added that he wasn’t worried if the Chinese stop buying U.S. Treasuries because someone else will do so instead. His comments followed the president’s overnight threat to raise “$100 billion of additional tariffs” on imports from China. (From the context and subsequent remarks, it seems that President Trump probably meant raising tariffs on $100 billion of Chinese imports, although we can't be certain). U.S. imports from China last year totaled $524 million.
The immediate numbers don’t explain the market reaction. Total U.S. exports to China last year were just $187 billion, or about 1% of the U.S. economy.
The chaos is the story. In the past few days different voices from the administration have said a trade war is in the cards, it isn’t in the cards, there are already talks behind the scenes, there aren’t talks, the president is open to negotiation, and he’s playing hardball. FINRA said recently that stock-market margin debt - the value of stocks owned with borrowed money - is near record levels of around $650 billion.
But who wants to be long the market, with borrowed money, over a weekend following these headlines?
Over the five-day week the S&P 500 fell 1.4% and the Nasdaq Composite 2.1%. Three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 lost value. Oil slumped 4.5% over the week, while gold firmed, adding 0.7%.
